source_text:
Fragmenta in epistulam ii ad Corinthios (in catenis)
2 Kor 1,1
Καὶ τὸ πρότερον αὐτοῖς ἐγκαλῶν οὐ μόνος ἐγκαλεῖ, καὶ νῦν καταλλαττόμενος οὐ
μόνος γράφει, τῇ τοῦ ἁγίου Τιμοθέου προσλήψει τὸ πρᾶγμα δεικνὺς ἀξιόπιστον.
κἀνταῦθα μὲν τὸ δι' οὗ καὶ τῷ πατρὶ προσήκειν ἔδειξε λέγων διὰ θελήματος θεοῦ. 2
Kor 1,1–2 Ἐπειδὴ ἐν τῇ προτέρᾳ ἐπιστολῇ οὐ μόνος ἐνεκάλεσεν, καὶ νῦν
παραμυθούμενος οὐ μόνος γράφει, ἀλλὰ τῇ τοῦ ἁγίου Τιμοθέου προσλήψει τὸ
πρᾶγμα δείκνυσιν ἀξιόπιστον. ἐπειδὴ δέ φησιν ἀπὸ θεοῦ πατρὸς ἡμῶν, ἰστέον ὅτι ἐπὶ
μὲν τῶν γεννητῶν καὶ θεὸς καὶ πατὴρ λέγεται, ἐπὶ δὲ τοῦ υἱοῦ μόνως πατήρ· τὸ γὰρ
ὁ θεὸς μοῦ καὶ ὁ θεὸς ὑμῶν ἐν σαρκὶ ὢν ὁ Χριστὸς ἔλεγεν. 2 Kor 1,3 Αὕτη ἡ δόξα ἣν
δοξάζει καὶ ἐπονομασίαις ἐπονομάζει τὸν θεόν, ἤδη τὸ τῆς καταλλαγῆς
προμηνύουσιν. πατὴρ τῶν οἰκτιρμῶν καὶ θεὸς πάσης παρακλήσεως· ἐπὶ γὰρ τῶν
γεννητῶν καὶ θεὸς καὶ πατὴρ λέγεται, ἐπὶ δὲ υἱοῦ μόνον πατὴρ ὁμολογεῖται. Οἰκείως
τοῖς θλιβομένοις ἀπ' οἰκτιρμῶν θεοῦ καὶ παρακλήσεως ἄρχεται, χρηστὰς αὐτοῖς
ὑποφαίνων ἐλπίδας· εἰ γὰρ πατὴρ οἰκτιρμῶν ὁ θεός, παρακαλέσειεν ἂν τοὺς δι'
αὐτὸν διωκομένους καὶ θλιβομένους. 2 Kor 1,4 Παρακαλῶν ὁ θεὸς καὶ
παραμυθούμενος οὐκ ἐπὶ μικροῦ τὴν παραμυθίαν ποιεῖται. Ταῦτα προανακηρύττει,
ἐπειδὴ ἔμελλε τὸν κατακριθέντα δι' ἁμαρτίαν ἀνακαλεῖσθαι διὰ τῆς παρακλήσεως. 2
Kor 1,6 Ἡ ἡμετέρα θλίψις ὑμῖν παραμυθία γίνεται· εἰ γὰρ οἱ ἀπόστολοι θλίβονται,
πολλῷ μᾶλλον οἱ λοιποί. ἢ καὶ τοῦτό φησιν· εἰ καὶ θλιβόμεθα ὑπὸ τῶν ἀνθρώπων
διὰ τὴν ὑμετέραν σωτηρίαν, τοῦτο πάσχομεν, ὅτι ὑμῖν κηρύττομεν τὸν Χριστόν. Ἐὰν
παραμυθίας τύχωμεν παρὰ θεοῦ δι' ὑμᾶς, ἵνα ἀρκέσωμεν πρὸς τὴν ὑμετέραν
παράκλησιν, ὥστε προτρέπειν ὑμᾶς πάσχειν τὰ αὐτὰ ἃ καὶ ἡμεῖς ὑπομένομεν
παθήματα. 279 2 Kor 1,7 Ἐλπίζω ὅτι τὰ αὐτά μοι ὑπομένοντας ὁμοίως παρὰ θεοῦ καὶ
τῆς παρακλήσεως τεύξασθαι. 2 Kor 1,8 Οὐκ ἐπιδεικνύμενος διηγεῖται τὰς συμβάσας
αὐτῷ ἐν τῇ Ἀσίᾳ θλίψεις, ἀλλὰ πρὸς ὑπομονὴν τῶν παθημάτων αὐτοὺς ἀλείφων.
Ἀντὶ τοῦ ὥστε ἀπαγορεῦσαι ἡμᾶς καὶ τοῦ ζῆν. 2 Kor 1,9 Ἀπόκριμα λέγεται ἡ ἀπὸ τοῦ
κρίματος ἀπόφασις. ὅσον οὖν τὸ ἐφ' ἑαυτοῖς· τὴν γὰρ ἀπόφασιν τοῦ θανάτου
ἐσχήκαμεν, δι' οὗ σωφρονιζόμεθα μὴ πεποιθέναι ἐφ' ἑαυτοῖς ἀλλ' ἐπὶ τῷ σώζοντι
θεῷ καὶ τοὺς ἑαυτοὺς ἀπαγορεύοντας. 2 Kor 1,11 Οὐχ ὡς φιλοσωματῶν διαφεύγειν
εὔχεται τοὺς ἐπιβουλεύοντας, ἀλλ' ἵνα ὑπηρετῇ τοῖς δοθεῖσιν αὐτῷ χαρίσμασιν,
ὅπως ἐκ πολλῶν προσώπων τῶν νῦν καὶ διὰ πολλῶν τῶν ἐσομένων εὐχαριστηθῇ τὸ
κήρυγμα διασῶζον αὐτούς· εἰπὼν γὰρ διὰ πολλῶν τὴν διδαχὴν τῶν ἐσομένων
ἀπέδειξεν. τὸ δὲ εὐχαριστηθῇ ὑπὲρ ὑμῶν ἀντὶ τοῦ ὑπὲρ ἧς καὶ αὐτοὶ τετυχήκαμεν
δωρεᾶς. 2 Kor 1,12α Τοῦτο ἡμῶν τὸ καύχημά ἐστιν ὅτι μαρτυρεῖ ἡμῖν ἡ συνείδησις
ἡμῶν ὅτι ὀρθῶς κηρύττομεν. 2 Kor 1,12β Καὶ μὴν τὴν σοφίαν τῶν ἔξωθεν ψυχικὴν
εἶναι βούλεται, ἀλλὰ νῦν αἰνίττεται ὅτι οὐκ ἐχρήσατο λόγῳ κατὰ τοὺς ἔξω· ἐφ' ᾧ τε
λαβεῖν τι παρ' αὐτῶν, οὐ σαρκικὴν ἔσχε τοῦ κηρύγματος τὴν αἰτίαν. 2 Kor 1,13–14
Οὐκ ἄλλα ἐδιδάξαμεν ὑμᾶς συνόντες ὑμῖν παρ' ἃ νῦν ἐπιστέλλομεν, ἀλλὰ ταῦτα ἃ
καὶ ἀναγινώσκετε ἀκαλλώπιστα ὄντα· ὅθεν καὶ ἐπιγινώσκετε ἡμῶν μὲν ἰδιώτην τὸν
λόγον ὄντα, τοῦ θεοῦ δὲ τὴν ἐνεργοῦσαν δύναμιν εἰς πίστιν. 280 Καύχημα λέγει τοὺς
Korινθίους ὁ Παῦλος ἑαυτοῦ ἐφ' οἷς κατώρθωσε κηρύξας· καύχημα δὲ τῶν
Korινθίων αὐτῶν ἐν ἡμέρᾳ Χριστοῦ ὡσανεὶ δόξαν ἐχόντων ἐφ' οἷς ἐδέξαντο τὸ
κήρυγμα. Ἐλπίζω ὅτι ἐπιγνώσεσθε, ἐπειδὴ καὶ ἤδη ἀπὸ μέρους ἐπέγνωτε ὅτι ἐν τῇ
ἡμέρᾳ τοῦ κυρίου καύχημα ὑμῶν ἐσμεν καθὼς καὶ ὑμεῖς ἡμῶν· οἱ μὲν γὰρ ἐφ' οἷς
κατόρθωσιν κηρύξαντες σεμνύνονται, οἱ δὲ ἐφ' οἷς ἐπίστευσαν τῷ κηρύγματι
φιλοτιμοῦνται. 2 Kor 1,17 Οὐ διά τι σαρκικὸν ἐλθεῖν ἐβουλευόμην ἀλλὰ διὰ τὸν
pass_a_gloss:
[Edition heading: Fragments on the second letter to the Corinthians (in the catenae). Label 2 Cor 1:1.] And when he was accusing them before, he does not accuse alone; and now, when he is reconciling, he does not write alone, by the taking-on of holy Timothy showing the matter to be worthy of trust. And here, on the one hand, he showed that the "through whom" also belongs to the Father, saying "through the will of God."
[Label 2 Cor 1:1-2; a second catena form of the same note. Its opening repeats the first form: since in the former letter he did not accuse alone, and now when consoling he does not write alone, but by the taking-on of holy Timothy he shows the matter trustworthy. Its new material:] But since he says "from God our Father," one must know that in the case of those who are born he is said to be both God and Father, but in the case of the Son only Father; for the words "my God and your God" Christ was saying while he was in the flesh.
[Label 2 Cor 1:3.] This glory which he glorifies, and with namings he names God, already announce beforehand the matter of the reconciliation. "Father of mercies and God of all comfort": for in the case of those who are born he is said to be both God and Father, but in the case of the Son he is confessed only Father. Fittingly for those being afflicted he begins from the mercies of God and from comfort, hinting good hopes to them; for if God is Father of mercies, he would comfort those persecuted and afflicted because of him.
[Label 2 Cor 1:4.] God, comforting and consoling, does not make the consolation on a small scale. He proclaims these things beforehand, since he was going to call back, through the comfort, the man condemned on account of sin.
[Label 2 Cor 1:6.] Our affliction becomes consolation for you; for if the apostles are afflicted, much more the rest. Or he also says this: if indeed we are afflicted by men on account of your salvation, we suffer this because we preach Christ to you. If we obtain consolation from God on account of you, it is so that we may be sufficient for your encouragement, so as to urge you to suffer the same sufferings which we also endure. [Page number 279 dropped.]
[Label 2 Cor 1:7.] I hope that you, enduring the same things as I, will likewise obtain from God the comfort as well.
[Label 2 Cor 1:8.] Not showing himself off does he relate the afflictions that happened to him in Asia, but anointing them toward endurance of the sufferings. In place of: so that we gave up even on living.
[Label 2 Cor 1:9.] "Sentence" is said of the verdict that comes from the judgment. So as far as it lay with ourselves: for we have had the verdict of death, through which we are brought to soundness of mind not to have trusted in ourselves but in God who saves even those who give themselves up.
[Label 2 Cor 1:11.] Not as a lover of the body does he pray to escape those plotting against him, but in order that he may serve the gifts given to him, so that from many persons of those now and through many of those who will be, thanks may be given for the preaching that keeps them safe; for by saying "through many" he pointed out the teaching of those who will be. And "thanks may be given on your behalf" stands in place of "for the gift which we ourselves also have obtained."
[Label 2 Cor 1:12a.] This is our boast, that our conscience testifies to us that we preach rightly. [Label 2 Cor 1:12b.] And indeed he holds the wisdom of those outside to be "natural," but now he hints that he did not use speech after the manner of those outside; and, with a view to taking something from them, he did not have a fleshly reason for the preaching.
[Label 2 Cor 1:13-14.] We did not teach you other things while we were with you beside the things we now write, but these which you also read, being unadorned; from which you also recognize that our speech is that of an untrained man, but the power working toward faith is God's. [Page number 280 dropped.] Paul calls the Corinthians his own boast for the things he set right by preaching; and [himself] the boast of the Corinthians themselves on the day of Christ, as having glory, as it were, for the things in which they received the preaching. I hope that you will come to know, since you already have come to know in part, that on the day of the Lord we are your boast, just as you also are ours; for the ones take pride for the things in which they succeeded by preaching, the others take honor for the things in which they believed the preaching.
[Label 2 Cor 1:17.] Not on account of something fleshly was I planning to come, but on account of the ... [sentence continues in the next section]
pass_b_english: On 2 Corinthians 1:1: When he reproached them before, he did not reproach them alone; and now that he is making peace, he does not write alone either. By taking holy Timothy as his partner he shows that the matter can be trusted. Here he also showed that “through” belongs to the Father as well, when he said “through the will of God.”

The second catena form adds: Since he says “from God our Father,” we should know that with respect to those who are born he is called both God and Father, but with respect to the Son he is Father only. For Christ said “my God and your God” while he was in the flesh (John 20:17).

On 2 Corinthians 1:3: The glory he gives to God and the titles he uses for him already announce the coming reconciliation. “Father of mercies and God of all comfort”: with respect to those who are born he is called both God and Father, but with respect to the Son he is confessed as Father only. To people in affliction it is fitting that he opens with God's mercies and comfort, letting good hopes show through; for if God is the Father of mercies, he would comfort those who are persecuted and afflicted for his sake.

On 2 Corinthians 1:4: When God comforts and consoles, his consolation is not a small thing. Paul announces this in advance because he was about to call back, by this comfort, the man condemned for his sin.

On 2 Corinthians 1:6: Our affliction turns into your consolation; for if the apostles suffer affliction, how much more the rest. Or he means this: if men afflict us for the sake of your salvation, we suffer it because we preach Christ to you. And if God consoles us on your account, it is so that we may be equal to encouraging you, and so urge you to bear the same sufferings that we endure.
On 2 Corinthians 1:7: I hope that you who endure the same things as I do will receive comfort from God just as I do.
On 2 Corinthians 1:8: He tells of the afflictions that came on him in Asia, not to show off, but to anoint them for enduring their sufferings. The phrase means: so that we gave up even on living.

On 2 Corinthians 1:9: A “sentence” is the verdict that a judgment delivers. So, as far as it lay with us, we had received the verdict of death. It brings us to our senses, so that we trust not in ourselves but in God, who saves even those who have given themselves up for lost.

On 2 Corinthians 1:11: He does not pray to escape those plotting against him because he loves his body. He prays so that he may serve the gifts given to him, and so that many people now, and many still to come, may give thanks for the preaching that keeps them safe. By saying “through many,” he pointed to the teaching that will reach those still to come. And “thanks may be given on your behalf” stands for “for the gift that we ourselves have also received.”

On 2 Corinthians 1:12: Our boast is this: our conscience testifies that we preach rightly. He holds that the wisdom of outsiders is merely natural, and here he hints that he did not speak as outsiders do. Nor did he preach for a fleshly motive, such as getting something from them.

On 2 Corinthians 1:13–14: What we taught you when we were with you is no different from what we write now. It is the very same, and you read it without ornament. From this you can tell that our speech is untrained, while the power that works for faith belongs to God. Paul calls the Corinthians his boast because of what he achieved by preaching to them; and on the day of Christ he is the Corinthians' own boast, since they will have glory, so to speak, for receiving the preaching. I hope you will come to see, as in part you already see, that on the day of the Lord we are your boast as you are ours. Preachers take pride in what their preaching achieved, and believers take honor in having believed it.
On 2 Corinthians 1:17: It was not for any fleshly reason that I planned to come, but because of …
notes: 2026-11-11 claude-sumfix-b3: retranslated from the locked Greek. The old English was a word-order gloss with misreadings (Timothy note, 'my God and your God', 'forbid us to live'), printed the 1:1 note twice and left 'consult/plan' side by side. Doublet collapsed: 1:1 (first form kept; the second form's new 1:2 sentence printed under 'The second catena form adds:'). The God/Father sentence repeated inside the 1:3 note is kept. Labels now one per note (1:1 to 1:17); page numbers 279, 280 dropped; section ends mid-sentence with '…'.

lemmas.note: the preposition applied to the Father, not only the Son

choices.english: he did not reproach them alone ... does not write alone
choices.why: Severianus explains why Timothy is co-sender; the old English misread this as 'regarding the previous reproach'.
rejected: Regarding the previous reproach to them

choices.term: τὸ δι' οὗ καὶ τῷ πατρὶ προσήκειν
choices.english: “through” belongs to the Father as well
choices.why: τὸ δι' οὗ is the phrase 'through whom' treated as a word; the point is that διά is used of the Father in 'through the will of God'.
rejected: that through which it was necessary for the Father

choices.term: τὸ γὰρ ὁ θεός μου καὶ ὁ θεὸς ὑμῶν ... ἔλεγεν
choices.english: Christ said “my God and your God” while he was in the flesh (John 20:17)
choices.why: τό introduces a quoted phrase; the old English made Christ 'the God of me'. John 20:17 has the words.
rejected: Christ, being the God of me and the God of you in the flesh

choices.english: second form printed only for its new 1:2 material, under 'The second catena form adds:'
choices.why: Brief rule: translate the first form in full; the second repeats the Timothy sentence word for word.
The God/Father sentence recurs inside the 1:3 note, attached to a different lemma (“Father of mercies”); it is part of that note's Greek, not a second form of it.

choices.term: Ἀντὶ τοῦ ὥστε ἀπαγορεῦσαι ἡμᾶς καὶ τοῦ ζῆν
choices.english: The phrase means: so that we gave up even on living.
choices.why: ἀντὶ τοῦ is the scholiast's 'stands for'; the old English turned it into 'forbid us even to live'.
rejected: so as to forbid us even to live

choices.english: even those who have given themselves up for lost
choices.why: object of σώζοντι: God saves even those who despair of themselves.

choices.term: ἐφ' ᾧ τε λαβεῖν τι παρ' αὐτῶν
choices.english: a fleshly motive, such as getting something from them
choices.why: ἐφ' ᾧ τε + infinitive states the purpose that would make the motive fleshly.
Printed ὑμῶν kept as written (a reading also found in New Testament manuscripts).
one rendering only; the old English printed 'consult/plan' side by side.
One label per note from the edition's 2 Kor labels; 1:12a and 1:12b joined under one 1:12 label; page numbers 279 and 280 dropped.
rejected: (2 Cor 1:1) style refs after the text

bible_refs.note: “my God and your God” quoted as Christ's words
